name: Clovis culture
title: The story of the Clovis culture

text: About 13,000 years ago, the Clovis people lived across North America.
People once thought they were the first Americans, but others lived there even earlier.
src: Clovis is the earliest widely recognised archaeological culture of North America, found from southern Canada to northern Mexico around 13,050 to 12,750 years ago

Older sites such as Monte Verde II in Chile show that Clovis people were not the first inhabitants of the Americas / For much of the 20th century many scholars held to “Clovis First”, the view that Clovis people were the first inhabitants of the Americas

text: They were hunter-gatherers who moved from place to place, carrying their tools hundreds of kilometres.
They hunted mammoths and bison, and also ate small animals and plants.
src: Its makers were highly mobile hunter-gatherers who carried fine stone tools hundreds of kilometres
relied on big game such as mammoths and bison, and also ate small animals and plants

text: Clovis points, their best-known tools, are stone tips with a long groove at the base.
They also made bone needles, probably to sew clothes from fur.
src: the Clovis point: a bifacial stone point, flaked on both faces and usually fluted on both sides by removing a long flake from the base
Bone needles from La Prele in Wyoming, made from jackrabbit, red fox and cat bones, were likely used to sew clothes from fur

text: They used red ochre, a coloured earth, and probably made beads from animal bones.
A boy buried in Montana was related to most Native Americans of today.
src: Clovis peoples, like other Paleoindian cultures, used red ochre / Clovis people are also thought to have made beads from animal bones
Anzick-1, a young boy found near Wilsall, Montana / he belonged to the same population as most modern Native Americans
